item.title: Nigerian legend King Sunny Adé took African pop music to the world’s stage
item.description: The ‘King of Jùjú’ embodies an impressive blend of cultural grounding, musical innovation, entrepreneurial insight and global acclaim.
item.content:encoded:
Sunday Adeniyi Adegeye, known as King Sunny Adé, is 80 this year. He has devoted more than 60 years of his life to influencing Nigeria’s popular music and promoting the unique sounds of jùjú music.

Jùjú is a Nigerian musical tradition that combines intricate rhythms, percussion, guitars, talking drums, call-and-response and Yoruba oral culture. It’s not only entertainment but a vehicle for expressing cultural identity, transmitting proverbs and praise traditions, and social life commentary.

Sunny Adé’s career embodies an impressive blend of cultural grounding, musical innovation, entrepreneurial insight and global acclaim. From his beginnings in Lagos to his rise as the globally celebrated “King of Jùjú”, his story is intertwined with the development of contemporary African popular music.

As a social philosopher, I regard Sunny Adé’s music as a tool for social change. This is because it transforms cultural expression into a medium of moral reflection and social engagement. His music communicates values such as communal responsibility, respect, humility, peace, diligence and integrity. It also draws attention to the social problems confronting Nigerian society.

I’ve argued that Sunny Adé’s music addresses social challenges, preserves Yoruba identity and promotes civic awareness, national unity and moral renewal.

item.title: ‘Swan Song’: Princess Diana’s brother’s book is icy in its contempt for the British royal family
item.description: Charles Spencer casts King Charles, then the Prince of Wales, as a petulant child and ‘bellowing buffoon jealous of Diana’s star power’.
item.content:encoded:
Revenge is a dish best served cold, so the saying goes. Charles Spencer’s new memoir, Swan Song, arrives nearly three decades after his sister Diana’s death, and it is icy in its contempt for both the British tabloid media and the “arrogance and entitlement” of the royal family.

Dedicated to “all those who have lost a sibling”, and billed as revealing “the true framework of Diana’s life”, the memoir has been marketed as “the most intimate, loving and honest portrait” of Diana yet.

However, the book is as much about Spencer as it is about Diana. Over 350 pages, his litany of grievances swamps the loving tribute he ostensibly set out to write. King Charles, then the Prince of Wales, is cast as a petulant child and “bellowing buffoon” who was “always extremely jealous of Diana’s star power”.

Among the most damaging claims is that Charles was “giddily elated” on learning of Diana’s death, a reaction Spencer attributes to Charles’ “pent-up contempt for Diana and his horror that the world was so bowled over by her death”, as well as what he sees as Charles’s relief at finally being free to marry the woman he loved.

“Rest assured,” Charles allegedly hissed, “we’ll forget [Diana] soon enough!”

item.title: Kolkata film institute suspends classes for sixth day after campus violence

item.content:encoded:
Classes at the Satyajit Ray Film and Television Institute in Kolkata were suspended for the sixth day on Saturday as students continued their “academic boycott” over an alleged attack by members of a Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh-affiliated organisation on the campus, reported PTI.

The RSS, a Hindutva organisation, is the ideological parent of India’s ruling Bharatiya Janata Party.

On September 27, at least six students were injured after being attacked for objecting to an event organised by members of the RSS-affiliated consumer group Akhil Bharatiya Grahak Panchayat.

The students’ union had stated that it was not informed about the event before the institute gave permission.

Poorvi Bondre, a member of the union, told Deutsche Welle that students confronted participants of the event after learning that the organisers were affiliated with the RSS and using the event to “promote its agenda” on campus.

“They called us anti-nationals and Naxals and attacked us with knives,” Bondre said.

Some students were also chased while others had their clothes torn and phones forcibly taken, the union had stated

Students have since been boycotting classes, demanding heightened security on campus and that those responsible for the violence be arrested, reported PTI.

The Kolkata Police is reportedly deployed outside the main gate of the campus.

item.title: ‘Love, fear, and a pursuit of fun’: What made Diksha Basu write a motherhood memoir
item.description: ‘This book began as my love letter to my daughters, and then it became a love letter to my mother.’
item.content:encoded:
I am a fiction writer. I find fiction safe, escapist, protective – a barrier against the world. It’s true, of course, that all fiction comes from reality and mine is no exception but I can always use an excuse with fiction when needed. When The Windfall was published, my mother insisted she saw my father on the pages and my father insisted he saw my mother on the pages. I quickly insisted neither of them was on the pages.

And now I sit on the eve of publishing my first longform nonfiction on one of the most vulnerable topics in the world – motherhood. And I have nowhere to hide. I find myself wondering why I wrote this book.

The now

Perhaps I wrote it out of self-defence. My daughters (currently eight and nine) and I do not yet have an emotionally complex relationship. There are emotions, there are fights, and there is growth and mirroring and a foreshadowing of the complications to come, but adolescence, while lurking, has not quite arrived yet. item.title: India proposal to end Russia war ‘most comprehensive’, says Ukraine
item.description: New Delhi had ‘for the first time’ signalled its willingness to ‘play a role’, said Kyiv.
item.content:encoded:
Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha on Friday said that India’s proposal to end the war with Russia is the “most comprehensive” and broad, reported RBC-Ukraine.

“For the first time, India has signalled its willingness to play a role,” he told reporters.

Sybiha said that Kyiv had also received proposals from Egypt, Turkey and the United States.

Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 triggered the deadliest conflict in Europe since World War II.

The Ukrainian foreign minister said that his country was prepared to agree to an energy and agricultural truce in the Black Sea. However, any energy truce must entail a cessation of attacks on all power infrastructure, including facilities at ports, he was quoted as saying.

Several vessels, including many with Indians on board, have been struck in the Black Sea in recent months.

Sybiha also said that Kyiv was considering an unconditional ceasefire along the frontline with Russia, RBC-Ukraine reported.

On Thursday, Russian President Vladimir Putin said that Prime Minister Narendra Modi had “very good ideas” for finding mutually acceptable solutions to end the conflict.

However, Putin ruled out an end to long-range strikes as Moscow intensified aerial attacks on Kyiv.

“We are told: ‘Let them stop striking your refineries, and you will stop striking their ships,’” Putin said. “It is simply ridiculous.”

item.title: October Indian nonfiction: New conversations about the past and the future in these recent titles
item.description: An actor’s memoir, a scientific guide to appetite and eating, the future of Indian languages, and more.
item.content:encoded:
All information sourced from publishers.

The World Was Not Their Story: An Odyssey of an Indian Reporter, Saeed Naqvi

With few correspondents overseas, independent India’s newspapers have depended on agencies and publications in London or Washington, content to wear the blinkers of the West. The world, in other words, was not their story. Saeed Naqvi spent his 60-year career trying to make it one. His journey began at The Statesman in the 1960s, where he made his name with an exclusive on the Beatles in Rishikesh and won Jayaprakash Narayan’s confidence while reporting the Bihar movement. Later, at The Indian Express, his association with Ramnath Goenka drew him into the paper’s battles and politics, especially during the Emergency.

After leaving The Indian Express in 1984, Naqvi founded the news agency World Report to put Indian journalists at the scene of global events. His reporting took him to 110 countries, often as the only Indian journalist there. He covered the 1971 JVP insurrection in Sri Lanka, the Sino-Vietnamese War and the TWA 847 hijacking in Beirut; saw Nelson Mandela walk free; interviewed Fidel Castro, Mikhail Gorbachev, Muammar Gaddafi and Israeli prime ministers; and reported from Iran during the Islamic revolution and Iraq during Operation Desert Storm. item.title: How a British police officer turned his Indian postings into pulp fiction
item.description: Edmund Cox’s tales of detectives and dacoits, which drew on three decades of policing, revealed the prejudices and hierarchies of the colonial state.
item.content:encoded:
As his 30-year career in the British Indian police drew to a close, Edmund Cox found himself confounded by a wave of burglaries rippling through the Bombay suburb of Bandora, now Bandra. The houses being broken into belonged to wealthy families who had abandoned them during the plague of 1896-’97. For some time, the police had no idea who was responsible. Then, two thieves were caught in the act.

Their confession, Cox recalled, stunned the police. They were Waghris, members of what the colonial government called a “criminal tribe”. Scattered across the suburbs, they used the “Baroda railway” to slip in and out of the city at will, committing crimes with impunity.

It was precisely the sort of episode that stayed with Cox: a crime, a chase, a community already marked out by the police, and finally the satisfying moment when the mystery was solved. Years later, these experiences would become the raw material of his books.

Cox had spent much of his working life moving through the Bombay Presidency and beyond. In My Thirty Years in India (1905), he looked back on assignments at Poona, Dharwad and Ahmednagar, moving between western and southern India, before going to Sindh and finally Thana. item.title: SK Bole – the social reformer who mentored Ambedkar but then joined hands with Savarkar
item.description: He helped build the legal ground for the Mahad Satyagraha and ended his career as president of the Hindu Mahasabha.
item.content:encoded:
On 4 August 1924, Sitaram Keshav Bole moved a resolution in the Bombay Legislative Council granting untouchables access to public water bodies, wells, dharmashalas, schools, courts and hospitals. Three years later, it was this resolution that was invoked by BR Ambedkar, a lawyer who would go on to lead India’s Dalit rights movement, as he led thousands of so-called untouchables to Mahad to drink water from a public water tank that had been barred to them.

The Mahad satyagraha was a critical moment in the anti-caste movement – a movement whose young leader, Ambedkar, had been mentored by Bole since 1907.

Just over a decade later, in 1938, Bole – a man who had worked for decades on behalf of underprivileged castes and classes – became president of the Bombay Provincial Hindu Mahasabha, a Hindu nationalist organisation. This contradiction at the heart of Bole’s life has gone almost entirely unexamined.

Since branches were established in Maharashtra from 1923, the Hindu Mahasabha there had been dominated by Brahmins. Its politics centred on the challenges its leaders perceived from other religions, particularly Islam. Caste reform, the abolition of untouchability and the concerns of farmers and labourers were never part of its core agenda.

item.title: ‘I try to write from within the body, acknowledging its innerness and mystery’: Poet Tishani Doshi
item.description: ‘Concepts that seem abstract – time, breath, rhythm – are all within the body, and they come into poetry,’ she added.
item.content:encoded:
Tishani Doshi’s latest collection of poetry, Egrets, While War, is a profound exploration of loss, angst, war, love and varied strands of life. And she engraves these moments on the rich tapestry of her exuberant language.

In a conversation with Scroll, Doshi discusses her ways of writing poetry and meditates on the purposes of art.

Many of the poems in this collection were published in magazines and journals. How did the book come into being?
When I write, I’m not consciously working towards a big project like a book. I usually work poem by poem, and there’s a great excitement in working on that small scale. Each poem is different, and honestly, I can’t say much about how things come to be because it’s a mystery. I’m afraid that by trying to crack open some kind of code, I’ll be breaking something. At some point, though, there is a tipping point. The poems become a gathering, and it feels like they belong to one another – they’re a family of poems and will go into a book. Usually, if I’ve been working for two or three years, certain themes emerge.

item.title: When does crowd control become ‘excessive’ police force?
item.description: India’s police manuals demand restraint and the bare minimum of force. So why do crackdowns from Jantar Mantar to Aarey Colony turn brutal?
item.content:encoded:
Among the questions the Supreme Court has asked the high-powered enquiry committee to answer on the Cockroach Janata Party protest crackdown, one has received more attention than others: did the police use “excessive force and violence” against protesters at Jantar Mantar on July 20?

The question undoubtedly merits attention. Going by the accounts of the petitioners, witnesses and human rights bodies, the clampdown was ferocious. Apart from batons and tear gas, the police allegedly used nail-studded lathis, rubber bullets, electric batons and even pellet guns. A Human Rights Watch report quotes a 24-year-old photojournalist as saying, “I have photos of protesters just standing there and the police beating them.”

But beyond the specifics of the protest at Jantar Mantar, there is another question in the Supreme Court order raised by the petitioners. What is “a proportionate and measured police response” to protests and peaceful assemblies that strikes an “appropriate balance between the maintenance of public order and the constitutional right to peaceful dissent”?

It is not hard to see the inherent conflict between the two mandates. Article 19(1)(b) of the Indian Constitution guarantees all citizens the right to assemble peaceably without arms, while Article 19(3) places restrictions on this very freedom in the interest of public order and the sovereignty and integrity of the country.

item.title: ‘I’m a little cockroach’: The new non-violence of poetry, protest, and imagined communities
item.description: In its joyous orality, the youth protest poetry cuts across class, caste, and gender precisely because of this mode of expression.
item.content:encoded:
Sab yaad rakha jayega, sab kuch yaad rakha jayega
Main Hindustan ki beti hoon
I am a little cockroach.


A people may coexist; a community must be imagined into being. And what more powerful tool of the imagination than poetry? Mesmerised by the flood of poetry streaming into my social media, I have put together a very preliminary sense of what the poetry of the Cockroach Janta Party protests did and is doing, and what kind of “Imagined Community” it is speaking into being.

The many commentaries and thoughtful publications that have emerged in the wake of these protests are a testament to an urgency – to note and remember and archive their unexpected and singular nature. To all these, I want to add the power of poetry in its active refusal of the politics of violence, and its creation of what Benedict Anderson would have called an imagined community that harks back to the imaginaries of the freedom struggle.

It looks towards a future by building on the ways in which the protests against the Citizenship Amendment Act in 2019 integrated that vision and voice in their poems and art. item.title: Nutrients in food mimic calorie restrictions. Can they improve our health?
item.description: Research in humans has yet to show that compounds reproduce the effects of calorie restriction or extend healthspan.
item.content:encoded:
Scroll through social media and you will soon encounter advice about living longer, from fasting plans and supplements to elaborate daily routines. Yet reaching an advanced age tells us little about how healthy or independent those later years will be.

Researchers often use the term healthspan for the years spent in good health, free from disability or chronic disease. In 2021, global life expectancy was 71.4 years, while healthy life expectancy was 61.9 years, according to the World Health Organization (WHO). That represents a gap of nine and a half years. A separate analysis estimated that this gap widened in 203 of 204 countries and territories between 1990 and 2023.

The WHO takes a broader view of healthy ageing, focusing on the abilities that allow people to do what they value, such as undertaking daily tasks, maintaining relationships and contributing to society. This recognises that people can live well while managing a health condition. “Functional healthspan” describes how long someone maintains the capacities needed for independent living.

As we age, declining muscle strength and mass, reduced aerobic fitness and even “inflammaging” (or low-grade inflammation) become more prevalent. These changes vary considerably between people. Diet, physical activity and sleep can influence how well we age, although income, housing, healthcare and the wider environment also play important roles.

item.title: How ‘new’ is the tilcayo, the first cat species to be discovered in a 100 years?
item.description: Researchers knew of a tiger cat occurred in Bolivia’s Yungas cloud forests, but it had never been formally described.
item.content:encoded:
Scientists have described a species of tiger cat that was previously unknown to science. From Bolivia’s Yungas cloud forests, it is the first discovery of a living novel cat species in more than 100 years.

The tilcayo (Leopardus tilcayo) takes its species name from the name locals already had for it. Paola Nogales-Ascarrunz, a National Geographic explorer who discovered the species and co-author of the Current Biology paper that describes it, said the name honors traditional knowledge in the region.

The tilcayo is smaller than a domestic cat at 1.4 kilograms (3 pounds). It has rounded ears, a slender body and a coat with large spots.

“I have the honor of naming a cat, and that’s a really big thing,” Nogales-Ascarrunz, who is also a researcher at the Universidad Mayor de San Andrés in La Paz, Bolivia, told Mongabay by phone.

item.title: From Azad Hind Radio to Gandhi: The forgotten Indian story of Surinamese composer Majoie Hajary
item.description: The pianist with Indian roots moved from wartime radio and New Delhi to ragas, devotional music and one of the most unusual Gandhi recordings of the 1960s.

Any serious conversation about Gandhi and music would be incomplete without discussing a French record from 1968. Requiem pour Mahatma Gandhi was composed by Majoie Hajary, who was born in Suriname, trained in Amsterdam and Paris, spent time in New Delhi and moved throughout her life between musical worlds that others had preferred to keep apart.

Hajary was born in 1921 in Paramaribo, capital of the Dutch colony of Suriname in South America. While her father was born in Suriname, her paternal grandparents had come from India. Her mother was Afro-Chinese. Her ancestors had come to the colony as indentured labourers.

Hajary grew up in comfort, principally with Western classical music at home.

Ellen de Vries, author of the 2025 Hajary biography Surinaamse Rapsodie and the researcher behind a website about the composer, majoiehajary.org, helped fill in some of the gaps in Hajary’s Indian story.

item.title: ‘Digger’ review: Extra-large and super-thin satire digs deep for rare gold
item.description: Tom Cruise leads Alejandro Gonzalez Inarittu’s black comedy about climate change.
item.content:encoded:
If you can’t defeat them, satirise them – this attitude towards the enemies of the environment has been embraced by filmmakers. Snowpiercer, Don’t Look Up and Mickey 17 have all mined comedy out of melting icecaps and vanishing habitats. Alejandro Gonzalez Inarittu’s Digger joins the doomsday club with a wildly swinging, noisy shovel.

The film stars a bunch of excellent actors audibly chomping on the scenery, led by a ravenous Tom Cruise. Having saved the world umpteen times, Cruise entertainingly plays a mega-agent of mass destruction.

item.title: The start of a run can feel like a fight against your body – and that is normal
item.description: This sensation is actually caused by a normal feature of human physiology.
item.content:encoded:
Many runners describe the first ten to 15 minutes of a run as the hardest of all. Breathing can feel laboured, the legs can feel heavy and a pace that would normally seem manageable may suddenly feel surprisingly difficult.

It might be easy to assume the reason your run feels so difficult at the start is because you’re not fit enough. But in reality, this sensation is actually caused by a normal feature of human physiology – and one that affects almost everyone, from someone attempting their first 5K to elite endurance athletes.

One way I often explain this phenomenon to athletes and students is that when you begin running, an argument starts between your muscles and your cardiorespiratory system. While there’s nothing we can do to stop this quarrel from happening, there are many things we can do to help the body find a resolution more quickly in the future.

The moment you start running, your working muscles demand a rapid supply of energy almost instantly. Yet the system responsible for producing that energy from oxygen cannot respond quite as quickly.

For Tyeb Mehta, the line was never merely a formal device. It carried philosophical and emotional weight, embodying memory, myth, pain and redemption, with an intensity that was both provocative and contemplative. It is through his drawings that we trace the paradox at the heart of his practice: that the instability we perceive on his canvases was carefully engineered.

Mehta’s drawings have piqued visitors to the retrospective Tyeb Mehta: Bearing Weight (with the lightness of being). Largely unseen for decades, they facilitate fresh curatorial perspectives on his visual language. We seldom see an artist’s preliminary exercises or the evolutionary charting of a creative practice. Mehta’s early drawings reveal an artist deeply invested in form and demonstrate the experiments he undertook to break and contort this form from within, long before these concerns found their fullest expression in his paintings. item.title: Rohingya genocide: ICJ will soon issue ruling on case against Myanmar
item.description: The ruling could strengthen the case for a formal recognition from Myanmar of the Rohingya and the restitution of their citizenship rights.
item.content:encoded:
The International Court of Justice is reportedly going to rule in the coming weeks in The Gambia v. Myanmar, the genocide case against Myanmar.

In 2019, The Gambia filed an application at the ICJ alleging that Myanmar had violated the United Nations’ 1948 Genocide Convention in its treatment of the Rohingya people.

The Rohingya aren’t from The Gambia, and no atrocities against them took place there. But, under international law, any state can file a case with the ICJ if it believes a country has violated the convention. This was confirmed by the court in a 2022 decision against Myanmar’s attempt to block the case on jurisdictional grounds.

Who are the Rohingya?

The Rohingya are an ethnic minority group that have long lived in the Arakan region of western Myanmar, which today corresponds to the Rakhine state.

As Muslims in an overwhelmingly Buddhist country, the Rohingya have often experienced discrimination and persecution. Most notably, in 1982, Myanmar passed a law that removed the Rohingya from a list of ethnic groups eligible for citizenship.

As a result, most Rohingya lost their citizenship, and with it, their most basic rights and freedoms. The ICJ case, however, concerns the campaign of violence conducted by the Myanmar military against the Rohingya that began in 2016.

Protests by residents of the Siang basin in Arunachal Pradesh against a proposed multipurpose dam intensified on Wednesday, as demonstrators clashed with security personnel and set a police vehicle on fire during Chief Minister Pema Khandu’s visit to Yingkiong in Upper Siang district, the Hindustan Times reported.

Residents of the Siang basin have opposed the Siang Upper Multipurpose Project for several years. Members of the Adi tribe, who live in the basin, have maintained that the project threatens their land and way of life. The protests intensified after the government began deploying Central Armed Police Forces for the pre-feasibility survey of the proposed project.

The Siang river flows into Arunachal Pradesh from Tibet, and is the main tributary of the Brahmaputra. The river is the site of the proposed 11,000 MW Siang Upper Multipurpose Project, described to be India’s largest dam.

On Monday, villagers and security personnel clashed in Geku during protests against the project and the deployment of Central Armed Police Forces for the pre-feasibility survey, Arunachal24 reported. Four persons were arrested in connection with the incident.

As tensions rose on Wednesday, protesters allegedly entered and vandalised the residence of Tuting-Yingkiong MLA Alo Libang in Yingkiong. Several government vehicles were also reportedly damaged.

item.title: Eggs, chicken could cost more as maize shortage due to ethanol blending will worsen amid poor rain
item.description: Nearly three-fourths of the ethanol produced in India currently comes from grains, particularly maize.
item.content:encoded:
Despite a record maize production last year, India’s poultry farmers are contending with higher retail prices of the poultry staple due to its increasing demand for ethanol blending. With a decline in sowing and deficient rainfall this year, experts say this is likely to get worse.

Maize was available to poultry farmers for Rs 12-14 per kg around the year 2019 but it now sells for Rs 27- Rs 28 per kg in the retail market. Since maize is the primary, starch-heavy food for all poultry and soymeal is the secondary food, farmers maintaining egg-layer and broiler poultry are both facing a crisis. They have to buy feed at these high prices and either pass on the cost to the consumer or bear the losses.

The contribution of maize towards ethanol blending increased from 0% in 2021-’22 to around 37% in 2025-26. India’s move to blend 20% ethanol in petrol has been a subject of much discussion this past year after vehicle owners alleged damage due to the biofuel. Besides, when sugar prices surged recently, it led to debate on whether it was due to the Ethanol Blended Petrol programme.

As I sat in his car and watched the city through the windows, I remembered how I had marvelled at those neem trees and those red brick buildings when I first arrived in the city as an undergraduate, and how much I now missed those happy, carefree days. External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar has warned that there may be a “major food crisis” in the coming months amid fertiliser shortages and disruptions in grain shipments caused by the wars in Ukraine and West Asia.

On top of it, “there’s the super El Niño”, said Jaishankar while speaking at an event hosted at Asia Society in New York on Monday.

The El Niño phenomenon involves the warming of ocean surface temperatures in the eastern and central Pacific. It typically occurs every few years and has been linked to crop damage, fires and flash floods.

On Tuesday, the Union government revised its food grain production target to 373.9 million tonnes for 2026-’27, which is 2.6 million tonnes lower than the estimated output in 2025-’26, reported The Indian Express. The decision was taken in view of the situation created by El Niño, said Union Agriculture Minister Shivraj Singh Chouhan.

item.title: The Indian state has made Bengali Muslims outsiders in their own land
item.description: Documents are meaningless with ethno-linguistic identity reason enough for arbitrary detention and even deportation of marginal workers across India.
item.content:encoded:
Reading news reports in recent weeks has made one thing clear: being a Bengali-speaking Muslim has, by itself, become incriminating in today’s India.

Simply having this ethno-linguistic identity is enough to trigger the suspicion of state officials. Amid the fervid political rhetoric about “ghuspetiya” – infiltrators – and supposed demographic change, being a Bengali-speaking Muslim has come to be associated with being an outsider.

Across the country, Bengali-speaking Muslim marginal workers are being picked up for questioning, detained and even deported to Bangladesh. For instance, last month in Bengaluru, 3,000-odd Bengali Muslim garbage and waste workers were picked up by the police as part of a massive verification drive against allegedly unauthorised migrants.

Only 31 of them were eventually determined to be Bangladeshi nationals and sent to West Bengal to be deported to Bangladesh. In Chhattisgarh, 23 workers from West Bengal – only one Hindu and the rest Muslims – were detained on suspicion of being Bangladeshi nationals this month.

In July, a Muslim woman tracing her roots to North 24 Parganas district of West Bengal was detained and deported to Bangladesh in July.

These three episodes are a continuation of a phenomenon that began last summer, when the authorities detained thousands of Bengali Muslim workers across the country, deporting hundreds to Bangladesh – mostly without trial...

In March 2022, Rahul Kumar’s family hired a nurse from a private agency to assist him for three days.

Kumar had been diagnosed with a motor neurone disease five years earlier. He was in his late thirties, and had begun losing sensation in his toes. Before long, he found it difficult to lift or move his feet.

While doctors did not immediately understand the cause of these symptoms, a series of diagnostic tests helped rule out possibilities such as inflammation from allergies and heavy metal toxicity. Neurological examinations eventually pinpointed his ailment.

Doctors told Kumar that the disease would cause muscles that control activities like walking, speaking, swallowing and breathing to weaken over months or years. Its progression could not be predicted, and it could not be cured. All he could hope to do through treatment was manage the symptoms.

Within five years, Kumar had become wheelchair-bound and dependent on caregivers to support his daily needs. His family hired a full-time helper who could assist him with everyday activities, as well as typing on a computer and phone. In March 2022, the family hired the home nurse from a private agency because the regular helper was unavailable. The service cost them Rs 8,300.

item.title: Days to go for polling, Brazil sees a lackluster election campaign
item.description: President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva is running against Flávio Bolsonaro, the son of incarcerated former President Jair Bolsonaro.
item.content:encoded:
With less than two weeks to go before voters head to the polls on Oct. 4, 2026, Brazil is experiencing a presidential election campaign that is much less heated than many would expect given the high-level of polarisation in the country.

The latest polling also suggest few shifts in the political landscape, dominated by incumbent President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and his main right-wing challenger, Flávio Bolsonaro, the son of incarcerated former President Jair Bolsonaro.

But making predictions about Brazil’s presidential vote is a tricky business. In Brazil, voting is mandatory for literate citizens between 18 and 70 years of age, and if one presidential candidate doesn’t get to 50%+1 of the valid votes (not counting absentees and blank or invalid votes) in the first round, the field is narrowed to two candidates, who then face a run-off, scheduled for October 25, 2026.

The run-off is a very likely scenario in the current situation. But as a political scientist who has studied Brazilian elections for decades, I don’t think it’s safe at the moment to base analyses on existing second-round simulations, since about 30% of voters are still undecided in the first round, if spontaneous polls are to be trusted. item.title: In Pakistan, attack on mosque and its fallout reveals evolving landscape of extremist outfits
item.description: The incident has reopened the cycle of Pakistani cross-border action and Afghan retaliation.
item.content:encoded:
The suicide bombing and gun attack that killed dozens in northwest Pakistan on September 18, 2026, highlighted the fragile security situation in the South Asian country. But it also shone a light on the complex and evolving extremism landscape there and the strained relationship between Pakistan and neighboring Afghanistan.

The assault took place as worshipers gathered for Friday prayers in the city of Kohat, in Khyber Puktunkhwa province, northwest Pakistan. A suicide bomber rammed an explosives-laden car through the wall of a police complex in the city of Kohat, targeting the mosque inside. Gunmen then exchanged fire with law enforcement officials during a 20-hour standoff. In all, 31 people were killed, including 16 police officers, while over 100 people were reported injured.

Supporters of the militant group Ittehad-ul-Mujahideen Pakistan, or IMP, claimed responsibility on encrypted apps like Telegram. But other seemingly aligned groups distanced themselves from the attack. Pakistan responded by conducting airstrikes in Afghanistan, home to at least one of the gunmen.

Over the past two years, we have conducted fieldwork in this region and closely monitored the operational and propaganda activity of violent extremist groups, including the Ittehad-ul-Mujahideen Pakistan. The attack and its fallout reveal much about the state of collaboration and friction among the various militant entities that have fueled violence.

item.description: Both the officials were accountants, the ministry stated.
item.content:encoded:
Two home ministry officials were arrested on Monday for allegedly seeking a bribe from an association in return for facilitating its pending registration under the Foreign Contribution Regulation Act.

Registration under the Act is mandatory for non-profit organisations to receive foreign funds.

One of the officials was posted in the ministry’s Foreigners Division, while the other worked in a Pay and Accounts Office and had previously been posted in the Foreigners Division, the Ministry of Home Affairs stated on Tuesday. Both officials were accountants.

“Preliminary questioning indicates that they were in contact with certain associations for facilitating their registration and renewal in lieu of illegal gratification,” the ministry added.

The investigation is underway.

item.description: Vinod Adani, accused of violating public float rules by investing in Adani Group companies through two foreign portfolios, was also cleared.
item.content:encoded:
The Securities and Exchange Board of India on Monday cleared Adani Group chairperson Gautam Adani, four companies of the conglomerate and 13 others in proceedings related to alleged violation of minimum public shareholding norms by paying a settlement amount of Rs 1.4 crore.

In India, listed companies must maintain a minimum public shareholding of 25%.

The securities market regulator had initiated proceedings against Adani Enterprises, Adani Power, Adani Ports and Special Economic Zone, and Adani Transmission, now known as Adani Energy Solutions, as well as their directors, after receiving complaints in June 2020 and July 2020 that they had failed to comply with the rule.

In its settlement order, SEBI has not made any mention of the ‌regulatory ⁠finding on the alleged violations.

The proceedings were part of the 24 investigations that the regulator undertook against the Adani Group after American short-seller Hindenburg Research published a report in January 2023 accusing the Adani Group of pulling off the “largest con in corporate history” through accounting fraud, money laundering and stock price manipulation, reported Reuters.

The Adani Group rejected the allegations, but the report pummelled the stocks of its listed companies and wiped out more than $100 billion of investors’ money at the time.

item.title: Gangster Goldy Brar added to US 10 most wanted list
item.description: The United States law enforcement agency increased the reward to $1 million from $50,000 for information leading to his arrest.
item.content:encoded:
The United States Federal Bureau of Investigation on Monday added fugitive gangster Satinderjeet Singh, also known as Goldy Brar, to its 10 most wanted list.

The agency also increased the reward to $1 million from $50,000 for information leading to his arrest.

Brar is wanted for his alleged involvement in the Lawrence Bishnoi organised crime group, which is accused of violent crimes in southern California, and across the US and Canada, the FBI said.

He is alleged to be a leader of the group in North America.

The FBI said that Brar is considered armed and dangerous and an escape risk. The law enforcement agency warned the public to “avoid interaction” with him.

The US authorities have charged Brar with conspiracy to run a criminal organisation, extortion-related offences and drug trafficking.

A federal arrest warrant was issued for Brar on July 1, and charges against him were announced on July 7 as part of a wider crackdown on three India-based gangs.

One of the indictments focuses on the Bishnoi enterprise, a criminal organisation led by gangster Lawrence Bishnoi.

According to the indictment, Brar allegedly helped Bishnoi direct members and associates of the organisation around the world.

The indictment also alleges that Bishnoi and Brar ordered the 2023 killing of Khalistani separatist leader Hardeep Singh Nijjar in Canada.

The Instagram account of political cartoonist Satish Acharya has been restricted in India after the Meta-owned platform received a legal request from the government.

A message displayed by the platform when users try to access the account says: “We reviewed it against our policies and conducted a legal and human rights assessment. After the review, we restricted access to the content in the location where it goes against local law.”

Another political cartoonist, Manjul, also said that Instagram had restricted one of his works about the Election Commission to users in India “pursuant to a notice from the Government of India/Law Enforcement”.

Acharya’s account was blocked under the 2021 Information Technology Rules, which require social media platforms to remove “unlawful content” within three hours of receiving directions from the government or a court.
